summary_paraphrase: A boy wants someone to play the stone game diketo with him; his mother, father and brother are each busy, so he sits alone and then starts playing by himself, and his fun draws the whole family out to join him. A small blue frog, never mentioned in the words, follows and mirrors him on every spread.

beats.function: the wish to play, posed as a question
names the game and asks who will play
two more asks and refusals in the same pattern
low point: alone, no one to play with
his fun makes Dad stop digging
each family member in turn leaves their task and joins, reversing the refusal order
wordless spread of the family laughing together
many hands in the game; the wish is answered

humor_notes: Light: the frog's reactions (sheltering from soil, clinging to the door) and Jabu tumbling over laughing. The contrast of Dad's big hole and Jabu's small hole is a quiet visual echo.

repetition.description: Ask-and-refusal pattern: Jabu asks one family member to come and play, and the next line begins with 'But' and names what keeps them busy
repetition.why: three identical asks let a listener say the request with the reader, and the third refusal sets up the low point

repetition.description: Each refusal is undone in reverse: Dad stops his digging, Mama brings out the food she was cooking, the brother leaves his reading
repetition.why: the ending answers each refusal by name, so the resolution feels earned rather than announced

repetition.description: The big hole Dad digs and the small hole Jabu digs for diketo
repetition.why: a concrete echo that links the father's work to the child's play

notes: OBSERVED: a small blue frog appears on every story spread without a word in the text and mirrors Jabu's feeling (hugs a stone, hides, cries when he is alone, leaps when he plays).
OBSERVED: the turning point that Dad has joined the game is shown only in the picture (he kneels at the hole with stones) on spread 9; the words only say Mama brings food.
OBSERVED: the payoff spread 11 is wordless: a tight close-up of the whole family laughing.
OBSERVED: the diketo spread (2) and payoff (11) share the same warm yellow-blue background; refusal spreads use flatter cool colours.
OBSERVED: the last spread shows only hands around the game, placing the reader inside the circle of players.

strengths: a clear wish stated on the first spread
three-step refusal pattern a listener can join
the child's own action, not an adult's decision, turns the story
the resolution undoes each refusal by name
a silent companion carries emotion for pre-readers
weaknesses: the solo-play turn passes quickly (one spread) for a book about being alone
family members join without dialogue, so the reunion is told mostly through pictures

child_appeal_heuristic.label: Research heuristic — not validated
child_appeal_heuristic.rationale: Scores are the analyst's reading of the pages, not observations of children.

age_suitability.notes: Everyday family setting; loneliness is brief and resolved warmly. Diketo with small stones is a traditional game; no unsafe behaviour shown.

metrics.lexicon_note: direct_address and sound_words are lexicon counts: a floor, not a measure. direct_address counts second-person words anywhere, dialogue included — it is not narrator-to-reader address

repetition.end_rhyme_note: heuristic: consecutive lines sharing a final two letters

causal_chain.effect: his fun draws his father out

causal_chain.cause: one by one the family joins

ending.last_page_move: many hands around the game, seen from above

craft.writer_note: The resolution undoes the refusals in reverse order, and the child causes it by acting, not by asking again. A wordless joy page before the last page lets the payoff breathe.
